entry.heading: Chainsaw Man (Tatsuki Fujimoto)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life here is an ordinary one: food, a home, people to eat with, and the freedom to choose your own wants instead of having them chosen for you.

frames.aligns: Care for the poor and the "least"; sacrificial love; human dignity versus being used as a tool.
frames.concerns: Gore, sexual objectification, devils and contracts treated as normal, cannibalism as climax (ch. 96), suicide themes.

frames.aligns: Evil is real and deceptive (Makima as a false shepherd); found family; sin's consequences are shown.
frames.concerns: Demonic content in a heroic frame; a hero who is a devil-hybrid; lust as the main motive; profanity.

frames.aligns: Evil is real and deceptive (Makima as a false shepherd); found family; sin's consequences are shown.
frames.concerns: Demonic content in a heroic frame; a hero who is a devil-hybrid; lust as the main motive; profanity.

frames.aligns: Mercy to orphans and animals; warnings against arrogance and control over others.
frames.concerns: Nudity and lust, alcohol, devils (shayatin) as partners and pets, mutilation of bodies.

frames.aligns: Desire as the root of suffering; impermanence; endless rebirth of devils looks like samsara (our framing).
frames.concerns: Graphic killing; appetite treated as a hero's fuel; little stillness or release.

frames.aligns: Critique of labor exploitation, poverty and state power; sympathy for an abused, uneducated youth; queer side characters.
frames.concerns: Debate over sexualized female characters and Denji's attitudes; violence against women; the "male gaze" question.

frames.aligns: Strong warnings about manipulation; value of a stable home, meals and work; loyalty.
frames.concerns: Absent fathers and lack of moral teachers; crude sexuality and swearing; nihilism; cult imagery.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Absurdism, Pagan/occult imagery, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Hedonism (explored).

entry.heading: Jujutsu Kaisen (Gege Akutami)
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Self-giving love (Yuji, Nanami, Gojo give their lives for others). Dignity of each life: Yuji refuses to treat anyone as disposable. Grief and remembrance of the dead.
frames.concerns: Occult framework: curses, spirits, rituals and body-possession treated as tools. Graphic violence and gore. A cult portrayed approvingly by its members. Mei Mei / Ui Ui material.

frames.aligns: Clear evil exists and must be fought; repentance and responsibility after failure (Yuji after Shibuya); loyalty and sacrifice. A Christian anime blog (Beneath the Tangles) reads Higuruma's courtroom arc as a picture of judgment and loving the criminal (headline only).
frames.concerns: Spiritual-warfare concerns: the series treats curses, possession and summoning as a skill system. Demonic-looking villains as fan favorites. Heavy gore.

frames.aligns: Clear evil exists and must be fought; repentance and responsibility after failure (Yuji after Shibuya); loyalty and sacrifice. A Christian anime blog (Beneath the Tangles) reads Higuruma's courtroom arc as a picture of judgment and loving the criminal (headline only).
frames.concerns: Spiritual-warfare concerns: the series treats curses, possession and summoning as a skill system. Demonic-looking villains as fan favorites. Heavy gore.

frames.aligns: Courage, protecting the weak, patience in hardship (sabr), justice against corrupt elders.
frames.concerns: Sihr (sorcery) and summoning of spirits are a core mechanic. Body-stealing and possession. Graphic killing. Brief immodesty and the Mei Mei material.

frames.aligns: Many Buddhist motifs: suffering born of attachment and negative emotion (curses), impermanence and the inevitability of death, mudras, the "honored one" phrase. Yuji's acceptance of being one part of a larger whole.
frames.concerns: Buddhist imagery is used for battle powers and spectacle. The "honored one" line is spoken in arrogance. Killing is constant; the first precept (no killing) is rarely discussed.

frames.aligns: Critique of a closed, aging elite and inherited privilege; Maki's fight against a misogynist clan; Higuruma's critique of a rushed justice system; refusal to treat any person as disposable.
frames.concerns: Critics argue women are sidelined in the second half (Nobara's long absence; ANN review calls it "slightly yikes plotting"). Mei Mei / Ui Ui framing. Graphic violence to teens.

frames.aligns: Duty, sacrifice, loyalty, honor, respect for mentors (Nanami, Yaga). Clear villains. Responsibility for consequences.
frames.concerns: Authority and tradition are almost always shown as corrupt. Occult content. Gore and despair. Fan culture celebrating a villain (Sukuna) and a mocking "Nah, I'd win" meme culture.

entry.dominant: Dharmic (Buddhist) imagery, Existentialism, Might makes right (critiqued), Nihilism (critiqued), Pagan/occult (Japanese folk religion). The labels below are this entry's framing unless a source is named.

entry.heading: One Piece
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a free life spent chasing your own dream, side by side with friends who would die for you, and never bowing to anyone who claims the right to own other people.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; condemned when villains do it
Played as comedy; sexual coercion condemned
Alcohol and tobacco shown casually; drugs condemned

frames.aligns: Human dignity of every person; condemnation of slavery and of rulers who make themselves gods; self-giving love ("greater love has no one than this", John 15:13) in Ace and Kuma
frames.concerns: Fan service and leering played for laughs; constant drinking and smoking; violence as the default answer

frames.aligns: Clear good versus evil; false gods humbled (Enel); loyalty and courage
frames.concerns: A human hero becomes a "sun god"; undead and occult imagery; sexualized art and harassment gags; heroes as outlaws

frames.aligns: Clear good versus evil; false gods humbled (Enel); loyalty and courage
frames.concerns: A human hero becomes a "sun god"; undead and occult imagery; sexualized art and harassment gags; heroes as outlaws

frames.aligns: Justice ('adl) against oppressors; freeing slaves as a virtue; hospitality and keeping promises
frames.concerns: Alcohol and tobacco everywhere; immodest clothing and leering; a man worshipped as a god

frames.aligns: Compassion for suffering beings; letting go of hatred (Luffy rarely kills); impermanence of power
frames.concerns: Violence as the main way problems end; ambition ("King of the Pirates") as a life goal

frames.aligns: Anti-slavery, anti-racism, anti-aristocracy; gender-variant characters shown kindly (per CSM); found family
frames.concerns: Sexualized female designs and harassment gags; okama characters sometimes used as comic relief; critics' essays on Oda and women (Anime Feminist, seen in search)

frames.aligns: Loyalty, honor, duty, gratitude; strong fathers and mentors; good monarchs honored; courage against tyranny
frames.concerns: Outlaws as heroes; distrust of all government; gender-identity themes (Ivankov, Yamato) and how adaptations have localized them (Bounding Into Comics, seen in search)

lenses.label: Might makes right
lenses.stance: Critiqued, though power decides most fights

entry.dominant: liberty and anti-authoritarianism, classical virtue ethics (loyalty and courage), and a critique of hierarchy and oppression. "Anti-authoritarian" is drawn from Wikipedia's account of the themes. The labels "critical theory" and "expressive individualism" are our framing, not any source's.

entry.heading: Attack on Titan (Shingeki no Kyojin)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived freely and for the people you love, but freedom pursued through violence spreads the hatred it means to escape; the story asks the reader to keep looking for understanding even when the world is cruel.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice for others; human dignity of the enemy shown in the Marley arc; forgiveness scenes.
frames.concerns: Graphic gore; genocide carried out by the hero; a "devil" bargain as origin of power; little hope beyond death.

frames.aligns: Sin passed down generations and the longing for freedom invite gospel discussion (some Christian bloggers write "the gospel in Attack on Titan").
frames.concerns: Violence level; occult-flavored origin (pact with a devil); revenge as motive; possible nihilism.

frames.aligns: Sin passed down generations and the longing for freedom invite gospel discussion (some Christian bloggers write "the gospel in Attack on Titan").
frames.concerns: Violence level; occult-flavored origin (pact with a devil); revenge as motive; possible nihilism.

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed; loyalty and courage; the horror of killing innocents is not hidden.
frames.concerns: Mass killing of civilians by the protagonist; extreme gore; some romantic content and nudity of Titans (non-sexual).

frames.aligns: The cycle of hatred and revenge is the core theme; attachment and fear drive suffering; compassion breaks the cycle.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; despair; suicide imagery.

frames.aligns: Critique of ethnonationalism, propaganda and dehumanization; strong female fighters; anti-war ending.
frames.concerns: Critics say it can read as sympathetic to ethnic nationalism or as using Holocaust imagery carelessly; reported alt-right fandom; Mikasa's arc centered on a man.

frames.aligns: Courage, duty, sacrifice for homeland and comrades; loyalty; realism about human evil; respect for soldiers.
frames.concerns: Gore and bleakness; children as soldiers; authority shown as deceitful; heavy moral ambiguity; heroes who commit atrocities.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Utilitarianism, Might makes right (critiqued), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Expressive individualism (critiqued).

entry.heading: Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived for others. You protect the weak, honor the dead, keep promises, and pass your will to the next generation. A long or powerful life bought by harming others is worth nothing.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrificial love ("No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends", John 15:13). Mercy toward repentant enemies. Dignity of the family and of the dead.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence. Buddhist and Shinto spiritual imagery. Kagaya's self-detonation and the dream suicide, read against Church teaching on suicide (Catechism 2280-2283).

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil. Sin shown as a corrupting appetite. Redemption themes (Equip.org's Christian Research Institute reviewed the film under the title "Slaying and Redeeming Demons").
frames.concerns: Occult-style demon imagery, a demonic cult leader, afterlife pictures that differ from Christian teaching, gore.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil. Sin shown as a corrupting appetite. Redemption themes (Equip.org's Christian Research Institute reviewed the film under the title "Slaying and Redeeming Demons").
frames.concerns: Occult-style demon imagery, a demonic cult leader, afterlife pictures that differ from Christian teaching, gore.

frames.aligns: Family loyalty, care for a sister, patience (sabr), justice against oppressors, modest romance.
frames.concerns: Violence. Revealing outfits (Daki, Mitsuri) and red-light district setting. Polytheistic ritual imagery. Self-destruction scenes, read against the Quranic prohibition (4:29).

frames.aligns: The story draws on Buddhist ideas: attachment and craving (Muzan's clinging to life), karma, compassion for all beings, impermanence, a monk-warrior (Gyomei) and a rebirth-style epilogue.
frames.concerns: Killing is central to the plot, against the first precept. Demons are destroyed rather than released.

frames.aligns: Empathy for the marginalized. The demons' backstories trace harm back to poverty, abuse and neglect. Anti-authoritarian critique of Muzan's rule by fear.
frames.concerns: Mostly traditional gender roles. Silent, muzzled Nezuko. Mitsuri's fan service. Polygamy (Tengen) played lightly. The Rising Sun earring dispute and Korean historical sensitivities.

frames.aligns: Duty, honor and sacrifice. Hierarchy and respect for elders. Masculine protective virtue (The Federalist ran a piece on the series and masculinity; Daily Wire framed it as a simple story of good and evil. Both found, not opened). Strong family bonds and continuing the family line.
frames.concerns: Intense gore. Occult and demonic imagery for some religious conservatives. Comedic cross-dressing. The red-light district arc.

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Dharmic (Buddhist), Traditionalism, Collectivism (as loyal service), Stoicism.

entry.heading: My Hero Academia (Boku no Hero Academia)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent helping others without being asked, even at cost to yourself; and real heroism means reaching out to save the person no one else will, including the "villain".

content.framing: Mixed: Mineta's behavior is mostly condemned or punished by classmates; adult heroine costumes are neutral

frames.aligns: Self-giving love; mercy toward enemies; repentance and reconciliation of Endeavor with his family; dignity of the weak and of a Quirkless boy
frames.concerns: Heavy violence late; fan service around Mineta, Midnight and Mount Lady; vestiges as quasi-spirits

frames.aligns: "No one is too far gone" redemption theme (Beneath the Tangles); servant heroism; accountability for sin
frames.concerns: Occult-flavored inherited power and spirits; villains framed sympathetically; mild language

frames.aligns: "No one is too far gone" redemption theme (Beneath the Tangles); servant heroism; accountability for sin
frames.concerns: Occult-flavored inherited power and spirits; villains framed sympathetically; mild language

frames.aligns: Courage, protecting the weak, justice against corrupt authority, respect for mothers
frames.concerns: Revealing costumes and lewd jokes; romance outside marriage (very light); graphic killings

frames.aligns: Suffering caused by craving for status (Endeavor) and hatred (Shigaraki); compassion for the suffering "inner child" of the enemy; impermanence of power (Deku loses One For All)
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; hatred cycles shown at length

frames.aligns: Critique of a celebrity, profit-driven system; attention to abused children and outsiders; some trans characters; social reform at the end
frames.concerns: Mineta played for laughs; trans villain Magne is killed early; the series favors reform of institutions over deeper change (Anime Feminist essay, title "Pride policing and the conservative politics of My Hero Academia")

frames.aligns: Duty, discipline, mentorship, merit, family repair, institutions reformed rather than torn down, a clear good and evil at the end
frames.concerns: Sympathy for villains may blur moral lines; violence intensity; immodest costumes; LGBTQ characters for some families

lenses.stance: Explored (our framing plus Christian reviewers' reading)

entry.heading: Spy x Family (Tatsuya Endo)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is building a family, even an imperfect or "fake" one, and protecting the peace that lets children grow up without war.

content.frequency: Occasional; heavy in a few arcs
content.framing: Shown with consequences (Yor's work) / Neutral (spy action)

frames.aligns: Adoption and care for an orphan; self-giving love in the home; peace-making as a calling. Grade reason: strong pro-family core.
frames.concerns: Marriage begun as a deception; Yor's killing work played lightly in places; drunkenness (Missions 79-80).

frames.aligns: Love that grows through sacrifice; the family as a "little church"; grief for war's victims.
frames.concerns: Killing as a profession with little repentance shown (the tradition treats even killing in war as needing repentance, St. Basil canon 13); lying condemned. Grade reason: violence and deception sit at the heart of the premise.

frames.aligns: Adoption and orphan care (James 1:27); a father who protects.
frames.concerns: Lying in the home (Proverbs 12:22); comic violence by the mother; drunkenness, which many Baptists see as a concern even in comedy. Grade reason: real concerns, but views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Plugged In's reviewers call the series fun and say it encourages thinking about friendship and family. Adoption mirrors spiritual adoption (Romans 8:15). Grade reason: positive review from the tradition's main media guide.
frames.concerns: Plugged In flags deception, frequent violence, coarse language and "lightly bloody action," and notes other volumes can be more intense.

frames.aligns: Family as refuge; protection of children; love winning over a hard heart.
frames.concerns: Anya's telepathy and Bond's foresight may raise spiritual-warfare concerns, though framed as science; drinking and drunkenness (many abstain); lying. Grade reason: several holiness concerns.

frames.aligns: Common grace: real goodness in a secular world; duty and diligence; lawful authority versus private violence.
frames.concerns: Heroes' lies and killings rarely judged by the story; drunkenness. Grade reason: common-grace reading fits, with ninth-commandment concerns.

frames.aligns: The family as a vocation where ordinary service matters; the state's sword versus private violence.
frames.concerns: Lying as a way of life; assassins working "for the nation." Grade reason: family vocation central; concerns are discussable.

frames.aligns: Love of neighbor, care for the weak, peace emphasis; characters slowly grow toward goodness.
frames.concerns: Drunkenness (historic abstinence; holiness churches ask members to abstain); killing for pay. Grade reason: peace theme fits; alcohol varies across Methodist bodies.

frames.aligns: Found family; care for war victims; critique of war propaganda (Henry, Mission 99).
frames.concerns: Deception at the heart of the marriage. Grade reason: broad fit; content judged case by case.

frames.aligns: Henry's stand against war propaganda; the anti-war core; care for orphans.
frames.concerns: Violence is central to the heroes' jobs and often played for laughs; spies and assassins serve states; lying. Many conservative families avoid such media altogether. Grade reason: nonresistance conflicts with the premise.

frames.aligns: Strong family focus; parents who sacrifice; adoption.
frames.concerns: Drinking and smoking (Word of Wisdom); deception (Articles of Faith 13 on honesty); violence. Grade reason: family core fits, several standards touched.

frames.aligns: Peace and justice emphasis; critique of militarism and propaganda; egalitarian domestic roles; found family.
frames.concerns: Comic violence; Yuri's harsh interrogation played lightly. Grade reason: themes align; violence is the main concern.

frames.aligns: Care for the orphan; memory of war; a dissenter jailed for speaking truth (Mission 99).
frames.concerns: Lying and killing; secret police echo real history. Grade reason: themes fit; views vary across movements.

frames.aligns: Strong care for orphans; family duty; no sexual scenes reported by any guide consulted.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and drunkenness (Missions 12-13 likely; 79-80); unrelated adults living as spouses under a false marriage; killing for pay. Grade reason: several clear prohibitions touched.

frames.aligns: Duty (dharma) to family and nation; protection of a child; respect for elders and teachers (Henry).
frames.concerns: Killing and deceit as livelihood; drinking. Grade reason: duty theme fits; ahimsa and satya concerns.

frames.aligns: Compassion growing from a selfish start; suffering caused by war; right intention slowly replacing a mission-only mind.
frames.concerns: The first, fourth and fifth precepts (non-harm, false speech, intoxicants) are all touched by the premise. Grade reason: themes fit, conduct conflicts.

frames.aligns: Found family over blood; role-swap in domestic work; critique of militarism, war propaganda, secret police and elite schools.
frames.concerns: Yuri's sister fixation as a joke; harsh interrogations played lightly; Common Sense Media rates diverse representations "very little." Grade reason: themes align, with representation and consent notes.

frames.aligns: Human care, not faith, solves problems; reason and empathy; war shown as human suffering. Plugged In confirms no faith elements. Grade reason: close to the series' own humanism.
frames.concerns: Comic violence; Anya's telepathy is fiction, not pseudoscience presented as real.

frames.aligns: Two-parent home; discipline, school effort, good manners; duty; children protected.
frames.concerns: Marriage as a cover story; comic violence by the mother; dishonesty in the home. Grade reason: traditional form, untraditional route.

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Communitarianism (family and peace first), Traditionalism (family form), anti-war Utilitarianism and Pragmatism.

entry.heading: Death Note (Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata)
entry.confidence: medium for series facts, volume-to-chapter mapping and documented controversies; low for exact chapter numbers of individual scenes
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story shows a life spent claiming the power to judge others, and lets the reader watch where that leads. Ohba's own stated takeaway is: "Humans will all eventually die, so let's give it our all while we're alive" (Wikipedia, citing Ohba).

content.frequency: Constant (deaths every few chapters), mostly non-graphic

frames.aligns: The story shows the ruin of pride and of a man who makes himself judge of life and death. The innocent suffer from his "justice."
frames.concerns: Mass killing presented in a stylish way; suicides dictated by the notebook; occult death gods; the "Mu" ending denies judgment and afterlife.

frames.aligns: Plugged In and Christian reviewers read Light as a man seizing God's throne, and the ending as judgment on that.
frames.concerns: Spiritual themes, apple and Eden imagery, shinigami as supernatural beings; a dark tone. Plugged In tells viewers to be prepared for "spiritual themes, violence, and language" (anime).

frames.aligns: Plugged In and Christian reviewers read Light as a man seizing God's throne, and the ending as judgment on that.
frames.concerns: Spiritual themes, apple and Eden imagery, shinigami as supernatural beings; a dark tone. Plugged In tells viewers to be prepared for "spiritual themes, violence, and language" (anime).

frames.aligns: Strong theme that taking a life unjustly is grave; arrogance (kibr) leads to downfall.
frames.concerns: Killing by one's own judgment; a human calling himself god (a form of shirk in Islamic terms); suicide; the denial of afterlife at the end.

frames.aligns: Karma-like logic: Light's actions bring his own end. Attachment to power and self drives suffering. Ryuk's detachment echoes impermanence.
frames.concerns: Many deaths; the "Mu" ending can be read as nihilistic rather than as Buddhist emptiness.

frames.aligns: A sharp critique of vigilante "justice," the death penalty, mass surveillance and populist media.
frames.concerns: Flat female characters (AnimeFeminist); police torture-like methods shown as clever; no LGBTQ+ characters.

frames.aligns: Law and order matter; the police and a good father (Soichiro) are honorable; evil is defeated in the end.
frames.concerns: Glamor of a teen serial killer; disrespect of father and family by Light; the story's ambiguity about justice.

entry.dominant: Utilitarianism (critiqued), Nihilism (explored), Might makes right (critiqued), Christian (explored, mostly as imagery and structure), Existentialism (explored).

entry.heading: Naruto (Masashi Kishimoto, 1999-2014)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where you never give up, earn the recognition of others through effort and loyalty, and break cycles of hatred by understanding and forgiving even your enemies.

frames.aligns: Forgiveness of enemies, self-gift for friends, redemption of villains (Gaara, Nagato, Obito), the dignity of an outcast child.
frames.concerns: Comic nudity and voyeurism (Sexy Jutsu, Jiraiya). Shinto and Buddhist powers and spirit-summoning. Suicide in backstories. Revenge as a long-running motive.

frames.aligns: Grace before merit: Iruka accepts Naruto before he earns it (Beneath the Tangles reads this as Ephesians 2). Servant leadership.
frames.concerns: Chakra, "sage mode," summoning animals, reanimating the dead and a blood-ritual cult may read as occult. The Bible warns against necromancy and divination. Peeping and nudity gags.

frames.aligns: Grace before merit: Iruka accepts Naruto before he earns it (Beneath the Tangles reads this as Ephesians 2). Servant leadership.
frames.concerns: Chakra, "sage mode," summoning animals, reanimating the dead and a blood-ritual cult may read as occult. The Bible warns against necromancy and divination. Peeping and nudity gags.

frames.aligns: Mercy, patience (sabr), loyalty, care for orphans, keeping promises, rejection of revenge.
frames.concerns: Nudity gags and voyeurism. Alcohol and gambling played for laughs. Depicting deities and magic. Romance outside marriage is light, but crushes are a theme.

frames.aligns: The "cycle of hatred" mirrors teachings on suffering and craving. Six Paths imagery. Liberation by understanding rather than vengeance. Reincarnation of souls.
frames.concerns: Buddhist terms used as names of weapons and a villain's bodies. Violence is very frequent. Desire and attachment drive heroes too.

frames.aligns: An outcast's dignity, empathy for enemies, criticism of war, secret police and clan discrimination.
frames.concerns: Female characters sidelined or stereotyped (Sakura's arc, the marriage ending), fatphobic jokes, the Killer Bee stereotype, sexist humor, a hero's bloodline destiny, child soldiers as normal (CSM's flags).

frames.aligns: Loyalty, respect for teachers and elders, duty to community, courage, marriage and children at the end, inherited "Will of Fire."
frames.concerns: Crude humor and nudity gags, a "pervert" mentor shown as wise, drinking and gambling, occult-flavored powers, a hero who defies superiors.

entry.dominant: Dharmic (Buddhist cycle of hatred), Classical virtue ethics, Collectivism (village loyalty), Traditionalism. Lens labels are this entry's framing unless a source is named.

entry.heading: Dragon Ball (manga, 1984-1995)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one of joyful striving: train hard, keep getting stronger, enjoy the fight, protect your friends, forgive rivals and give former enemies a place at the table.

content.frequency: Constant in the second half; frequent in the first
content.framing: Endorsed (fighting as virtue), with deaths shown with consequences
Played for laughs; Roshi's lechery is mocked but rarely punished

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice for others; mercy to enemies; conversion of villains; fidelity of friends.
